    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariancancer.html">
      <content name="title">Ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Tube</span></span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Primary Peritoneal <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> is a disease in which abnormal cells in the body grow out of control and form a <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumor</span></span>. Ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is a cancerous <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumor</span></span> that forms in the tissues of an ovary. The ovaries are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones.</p>What are the types of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are a few different types of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The most common type is epithelial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. It begins in the cells that cover the ovary.</p><p>There are also two related types of epithelial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> that can spread to the ovaries:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">Fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tube</span></span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tube</span></span><span class="qt2">. The </span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span> are a pair of long, slender <span class="qt1">tubes</span> on each side of the uterus. The uterus is the female reproductive organ where a fetus grows during pregnancy.</li><li>Primary peritoneal <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining the peritoneum. Your peritoneum is a tissue lining that covers the organs in the abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>These two <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span> are like ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, and they have the same treatments. So some medical experts also consider those two types as ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Some other rarer types of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> are malignant germ cell <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumors</span></span> and stromal <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumors</span></span>.</p>What causes ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes (mutations) in the genetic material  (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>Most ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span> are caused by genetic changes that happen during your lifetime. But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. Ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, including changes called BRCA1 and BRCA2. These two changes also raise your risk of breast and other <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Certain people are more likely to develop ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. They include those who:</p><ul><li>Have a family history of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> in a mother, aunt, grandmother, or sister</li><li>Have inherited changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes</li><li>Have certain other genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome</li><li>Have endometriosis</li><li>Took hormone therapy for menopause</li><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are tall</li><li>Are older, especially those who have gone through menopause</li><li>Have never been pregnant</li></ul>What are the symptoms of ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> may not cause early signs or symptoms. By the time you do have signs or symptoms, the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is often advanced.</p><p>The signs and symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, swelling, or a feeling of pressure in the abdomen (belly) or pelvis</li><li>Sudden or frequent urge to urinate (pee)</li><li>Trouble eating or feeling full</li><li>A lump in the pelvic area</li><li>Gastrointestinal problems, such as gas, bloating, or constipation</li></ul>How is ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>Will likely do imaging tests</li><li>May do blood tests such as a CA-125 blood test</li></ul><p>Often the only way to know for sure that you have ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is by having a biopsy of the tissue. A biopsy is done during surgery to remove the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumor</span></span>.</p>What are the treatments for ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery to remove as much of the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> as possible</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>Your provider may suggest that you have genetic testing to look for the gene changes that raise the risk for ovarian <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. Knowing whether you have the gene change may help your provider decide on your treatment plan.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hysterectomy.html">
      <content name="title">Hysterectomy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a hysterectomy?<p>A hysterectomy is surgery to remove the uterus (womb). The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. A hysterectomy treats problems like heavy bleeding, pain, or <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> in the uterus.</p><p>After a hysterectomy, you no longer have menstrual periods and can't become pregnant. Sometimes the surgery also removes the ovaries and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span>. If you have both ovaries taken out,menopause symptoms will usually begin.</p>What conditions does a hysterectomy treat?<p>Hysterectomy is a major surgery. Your health care provider may suggest other treatment options first. These might include medicine, hormone therapy, or procedures to remove fibroids or stop heavy bleeding. Sometimes these won't help, or surgery might be the only option, depending on the condition that needs to be treated.</p><p>Your provider might recommend a hysterectomy if you have:</p><ul><li>Fibroids, if you are near or past menopause, have large fibroids or very heavy bleeding.</li><li>Endometriosis, that hasn't been cured by medicine or surgery.</li><li>Uterine prolapse, which can happen after several vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity. It is when the uterus drops into the vagina.</li><li><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span>, of the uterus, cervix, ovaries, or endometrium (the lining of the uterus).</li><li>Vaginal bleeding, that is heavy or unusual and persists despite treatment.</li><li>Chronic pelvic pain, which starts in the uterus. A hysterectomy is a last resort since it doesn't fix some pelvic pain.</li><li>Adenomyosis, is a thickening of the walls of the uterus. A hysterectomy is only considered if pain is severe and no other treatments have worked.</li></ul>What are the different types of hysterectomies?<p>Your provider will discuss the type of hysterectomy you need, depending on your condition.</p><p>The different types of surgeries include:</p><ul><li>A total hysterectomy is the most common type and involves the removal of all the uterus, including the cervix. The ovaries and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span> may or may not be removed.</li><li>A partial (subtotal or supracervical) hysterectomy removes just the upper part of the uterus. The cervix is left in place, and your ovaries may or may not be removed</li><li>A radical hysterectomy removes all the uterus, cervix, and tissue on both sides of the cervix and the upper part of the vagina. This is most often used to treat certain types of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, such as cervical <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span> and ovaries may or may not be removed.</li></ul>What methods are used for a hysterectomy?<p>A hysterectomy may be done several different ways. Your provider will determine the best method for the surgery based on your general health, the reason for the surgery, and other factors.</p><p>Methods to perform a hysterectomy include:</p><ul><li>Abdominal hysterectomy. A cut is made in your lower abdomen (belly). Your provider may recommend this method if you have a large uterus or to check other pelvic organs for signs of disease. This surgery has a longer recovery time than the others.</li><li>Vaginal hysterectomy. A small cut is made in your vagina. This may not be an option if you have very large fibroids.</li><li>Laparoscopic hysterectomy. Uses an instrument with a thin, lighted <span class="qt1">tube</span> and an attached camera. This helps your provider see your pelvic organs. Small cuts are made in either your abdomen (belly) or vagina. This is not an option for all types of uterine fibroids.</li><li>Robotic surgery. Your provider guides a robotic arm to do the surgery through small cuts in your lower abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>After a hysterectomy, it can take four to six weeks to recover, depending on the type of surgery you have.</p>What are the risks of a hysterectomy?<p>Like all surgeries, a hysterectomy has risks, even though the results are usually good. Talk to your provider about the benefits and risks of having a hysterectomy.</p><p>More serious risks can include:</p><ul><li>Too much bleeding during surgery</li><li>Infection</li><li>Blood clots</li></ul><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/femaleinfertility.html">
      <content name="title">Female Infertility</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Infertility, Female</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Infertility means not being able to get pregnant after at least one year of trying (or 6 months if the woman is over age 35). If a woman keeps having miscarriages, it is also called infertility.  Female infertility can result from age, physical problems, hormone problems, and lifestyle or environmental factors.</p><p>Most cases of infertility in women result from problems with producing eggs. In primary ovarian insufficiency, the ovaries stop functioning before natural menopause.  In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the ovaries may not release an egg regularly or they may not release a healthy egg.</p><p>About a third of the time, infertility is because of a problem with the woman. One third of the time, it is a problem with the man. Sometimes no cause can be found.</p><p>If you think you might be infertile, see your doctor. There are tests that may tell if you have fertility problems. When it is possible to find the cause, treatments may include medicines, surgery, or assisted reproductive technologies. Happily, many couples treated for infertility are able to have babies.</p><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/uterinecancer.html">
      <content name="title">Uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Endometrial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that forms in tissues of the uterus, which is sometimes called the womb. The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy.</p><p>There are two types of uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Endometrial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is the most common type. This type of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> begins in the cells lining the uterus, known as the endometrium.</li><li>Uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">sarcoma</span></span> is a rare, more aggressive <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> that is harder to treat. This type of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> begins in muscle or other tissues in the uterus.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> usually happens after menopause. The cause is unknown. However, some factors and conditions that change the balance of hormones in your body may increase your risk. These can include obesity or metabolic syndrome (a group of risk factors for certain health problems).</p><p>Other factors and conditions that may increase your risk for:</p><p>Endometrial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></p><ul><li>Taking estrogen-only hormone therapy after menopause.</li><li>Having type 2 diabetes</li><li>Starting menstruation at an early age or menopause at a later age</li><li>Having never been pregnant</li><li>Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></li><li>Having polycystic ovary syndrome</li><li>Having a mother, sister, or daughter who has had endometrial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></li><li>Having certain genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome</li><li>Having endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the uterine lining)</li></ul><p>Uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">sarcoma</span></span></p><ul><li>Having had past treatment with radiation therapy to the pelvis</li><li>Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></li></ul>What are the symptoms of uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>The most common symptom of both endometrial <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">sarcoma</span></span> is abnormal vaginal bleeding. Both types of uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> may also cause pelvic pain or pressure, unusual vaginal discharge, or an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass.</p><p>Less common symptoms may include urinating (peeing) often, having trouble urinating, or pain during sexual intercourse.</p>How is uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>If you have symptoms of uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history and family health history</li><li>Do a pelvic exam</li><li>Order imaging tests</li><li>Suggest a biopsy or a minor procedure called dilation and curettage (D & C) to check the lining of your uterus</li></ul>What are the treatments for uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatment may depend on your health, how much <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> you have, and whether it has spread. The most common treatment is having a hysterectomy, which is surgery to remove the uterus. Sometimes the surgery also removes the ovaries and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span>.</p><p>You may have more than one type of treatment. Other treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Hormone therapy</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li></ul>Can uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There is no sure way to prevent uterine <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. But you can do things that may help lower your risk such as aiming for a healthy weight, getting regular physical activity, and talking to your provider about the benefits and risks of hormone therapy.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ectopicpregnancy.html">
      <content name="title">Ectopic Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Abdominal Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cervical Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Tubal</span> Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is an ectopic pregnancy?<p>The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy.  In an ectopic pregnancy, the fertilized egg grows in the wrong place outside the uterus. It usually occurs in the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span>. These tubes</span> carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus. Sometimes, an ectopic pregnancy can occur in the ovaries, abdominal cavity, or the lower part of the uterus (cervix).</p><p>Ectopic pregnancies can't end in a healthy pregnancy because the egg cannot grow. If the pregnancy continues, the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tube</span></span> can burst. This can cause internal bleeding, which can be a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate surgery.</p>What increases my risk of an ectopic pregnancy?<p>An ectopic pregnancy often happens because there is a problem with your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tubes</span></span>. But sometimes it's not clear why an ectopic pregnancy happens.</p><p>Factors that may increase your risk for an ectopic pregnancy can include:</p><ul><li>Previous ectopic pregnancy</li><li>Prior pelvic, abdominal, or <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">fallopian</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tube</span></span> surgery</li><li>Certain sexually transmitted infections (STIs)</li><li>Pelvic inflammatory disease</li><li>Endometriosis</li><li>Becoming pregnant while using an intrauterine device (IUD) for birth control</li><li>Becoming pregnant after a <span class="qt1">tubal</span> ligation</li></ul><p>Other factors that may increase your risk can include:</p><ul><li>Smoking</li><li>Being older than age 35</li><li>Infertility treatments</li></ul>What are the symptoms of an ectopic pregnancy?<p>You may not notice any symptoms at first. Or you may have some of the usual signs of pregnancy such as a missed period, breast tenderness, or nausea.</p><p>Early signs of an ectopic pregnancy may be light vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain. Ectopic pregnancy can be a medical emergency. Get medical care right away if you have these signs:</p><ul><li>Abdominal (belly) pain</li><li>Shoulder pain</li><li>Vaginal bleeding</li><li>Feeling dizzy or faint</li></ul>How is an ectopic pregnancy diagnosed?<p>An ectopic pregnancy can't be diagnosed without blood tests and an ultrasound. Your health care provider will do a pregnancy test to confirm that you're pregnant. They may do a pelvic exam to check for areas of pain, tenderness, or a mass.</p>What is the treatment for an ectopic pregnancy?<p>An ectopic pregnancy needs treatment to stop any damage to your organs. Your provider will use medicine or surgery to take out the ectopic tissue.</p><p>Losing a pregnancy can be devastating. An ectopic pregnancy is like a miscarriage, but it must be treated to prevent problems. People cope with grief in different ways. It may be helpful to discuss your feelings with your provider or a counselor. Many women who have had ectopic pregnancies go on to have healthy pregnancies later.</p><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>
